text.en: By the usual account, Placide Cappeau wrote the French words in December 1847, in a stagecoach between Mâcon and Dijon. Adolphe Adam set them within days, and they were first sung at Midnight Mass in Roquemaure that Christmas.
text.es: Según el relato habitual, Placide Cappeau escribió la letra francesa en diciembre de 1847, en una diligencia entre Mâcon y Dijon. Adolphe Adam le puso música en pocos días, y se cantó por primera vez en la misa del gallo de Roquemaure esa Navidad.

source.en: Denis Havard de la Montagne, "Minuit Chrétiens, une partition d'Adolphe Adam", Musica et Memoria, and "Origine gardoise du Minuit Chrétiens", Nemausensis (Nîmes, 2011)
source.es: Denis Havard de la Montagne, "Minuit Chrétiens, une partition d'Adolphe Adam", Musica et Memoria, y "Origine gardoise du Minuit Chrétiens", Nemausensis (Nimes, 2011)

text.en: John Sullivan Dwight, the Boston music critic and former Unitarian minister who wrote the English words in 1855, hated slavery. His line "Chains shall he break, for the slave is our brother" grows from Cappeau's French.
text.es: John Sullivan Dwight, crítico musical de Boston y antiguo pastor unitario que escribió la letra inglesa en 1855, detestaba la esclavitud. Su verso "Chains shall he break, for the slave is our brother" nace del francés de Cappeau.

source.en: George Willis Cooke, John Sullivan Dwight, Brook-Farmer, Editor, and Critic of Music (Boston, 1898), ch. VII, and Delaney Coyne, "The abolitionist history of 'O Holy Night'", America (26 November 2023)
source.es: George Willis Cooke, John Sullivan Dwight, Brook-Farmer, Editor, and Critic of Music (Boston, 1898), cap. VII, y Delaney Coyne, "The abolitionist history of 'O Holy Night'", America (26 de noviembre de 2023)
